walkthroughs.body_html:
Christianity through a Study of the Gospel of Matthew / Mark / Luke — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Christianity through a Study of the Gospel of Matthew / Mark / Luke brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Christianity through a Study of the Gospel of Matthew / Mark / Luke.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: When was the Trinity affirmed by council?
options: AD 33
AD 325

mcqs.q: Who developed the doctrine of original sin?
options: Aquinas
Augustine
Luther
Calvin

mcqs.q: What is the doctrine of the Trinity?
options: The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Christians believe everyone is reincarnated until they accept Jesus.
God is one being existing in three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) — distinct in person but united in essence; Christians remain monotheistic.
Christians believe in three different gods.

mcqs.q: What do Christians mean by resurrection, and how does it differ from reincarnation?
options: Resurrection and reincarnation are basically the same idea of life after death.

Resurrection is the once-for-all bodily raising to eternal life at the end of time (modelled on Christ's resurrection); reincarnation is the soul's repeated rebirth into new bodies. They are distinct doctrines from different religious traditions.
The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Christians believe everyone is reincarnated until they accept Jesus.

mcqs.q: What does the Buddhist doctrine of anatta teach?
options: Buddhists believe in a soul like the Christian or Hindu version.
Christians believe everyone is reincarnated until they accept Jesus.
Anatta means Buddhists have no personality.
There is no permanent, unchanging self or soul — what we call 'self' is a constantly changing flow of five aggregates (skandhas). This is distinctively Buddhist and differs from the Hindu atman.
